## How you work
You call tools; they run in the order you call them, and you see their results in your next response. There is no turn limit. You stop by ending a response without calling a tool. If a teammate tags you, or replies in a thread you're in, after you stop, you are woken and carry on.

## Execution environment
You have your own Python scratchpad file, scratchpad.py: you can read, write, edit and run it. Each run is a fresh Python process, and may take up to 6 hours; while it runs you see nothing on Slack, and what it holds in memory is lost when it ends. A run may use 5 GB of memory in all and write files of up to 8 GB each, and it may use multiprocessing with up to 2 worker processes (no more: it is killed if it has more processes at once).
Next to it is workspace/, a folder the whole team shares: every agent's runs can read and write it, and what one writes there the others can use at once. Put code and results that others can reuse there (for example shared code in workspace/tools.py, or results in workspace/results.json), import shared code with `sys.path.insert(0, "workspace")`, and say on Slack what you put there. Don't overwrite a file someone else wrote: write your own.
The Python environment includes NumPy, SciPy, SymPy, NetworkX, pandas, scikit-learn, gmpy2, Z3, mpmath and SageMath. Sage is imported in the same interpreter (`from sage.all import *`), and GAP and PARI work through it; Sage's Singular-based multivariate ideal methods (such as groebner_basis) crash here, so use SymPy's groebner for those.
There is no public internet access or web search. Do not try to access websites, remote APIs, or install packages. A run cannot start other programs, except more Python processes for multiprocessing.

## Slack
The team shares one Slack channel, #proof. slack_post posts to it, or replies in a message's thread; write @name to tag a teammate. slack_read shows what you haven't read, and after each response you are told when something is waiting. The lead, a person, may post too.
Use the channel to work as a team: split the work, and claim a piece before you start on it so that nobody duplicates it; keep the discussion of one piece in its thread; post each result as soon as it is checked (what was shown, and where in workspace/ its code is); and tag the teammate you need something from.

For each integer \(n\ge3\), consider smooth compact connected Riemannian manifolds \((M^n,g)\) with nonempty smooth boundary. Let \(\nu_g\) be the outward unit normal, let \(R_g\) be scalar curvature with the convention that the unit round sphere has scalar curvature \(n(n-1)\), and set
\[
\mathrm{II}_g(X,Y)=g(\nabla_X\nu_g,Y),\qquad H_g=\operatorname{tr}_{g|_{\partial M}}\mathrm{II}_g.
\]
Thus \(H_g\) is the trace, not the average, of the second fundamental form. Define
\[
c_n=\frac{n-2}{4(n-1)},\qquad L_g=\Delta_g-c_nR_g,\qquad B_g=\partial_{\nu_g}+2c_nH_g,
\]
where \(\Delta_g=\operatorname{div}_g\nabla_g\). Say that \(g\) has positive Yamabe type if the smallest eigenvalue of
\[
-L_gv=\lambda v\quad\text{in }M,\qquad B_gv=0\quad\text{on }\partial M
\]
is positive.

Require that \(g\) be locally conformally flat up to the boundary: every point has a neighborhood on which a smooth positive conformal multiple of \(g\) has zero Riemann curvature. No condition is imposed on the second fundamental form of the boundary. Also require that \((M,g)\) not be conformally equivalent to the round hemisphere
\[
\mathbb S^n_+=\{x\in\mathbb R^{n+1}:|x|=1,\ x_{n+1}\ge0\}.
\]
Here conformal equivalence means the existence of a smooth diffeomorphism \(\Phi:M\to\mathbb S^n_+\) and a smooth positive function \(\psi\) such that \(g=\psi^{4/(n-2)}\Phi^*g_{\mathrm{round}}\).

Determine exactly the set \(\mathcal D\) of integers \(n\ge3\) for which there exists one fixed manifold and metric satisfying all these conditions and a sequence of smooth positive functions \(u_i\) satisfying
\[
\begin{cases}
L_gu_i+n(n-2)u_i^{(n+2)/(n-2)}=0&\text{in }M,\\
B_gu_i=0&\text{on }\partial M,
\end{cases}
\qquad
\max_{\partial M}u_i\longrightarrow\infty.
\]

The answer is \mathcal D=\{n\in\mathbb Z:n\ge7\}. This was proved recently, so it is not an open problem: your team's task is to prove it, completely, and to write Python that really computes or checks every step that can be checked.
